title: Cross‑SDK transport presets and language examples for timeouts, keep‑alive, and pooling
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: SDK users across Python/TypeScript/Go are uncertain how to configure timeouts, connection pooling, and keep‑alive to meet production SLOs. Inconsistent examples and terse docs lead to both under‑utilized connections (wasteful short timeouts) and latent failures (overly long timeouts that block streaming or mask server disconnects).

Goal: Provide a set of recommended, tested transport presets (conservative, balanced, aggressive) with matching concrete examples for Python, TS, and Go; add explanations for streaming ergonomics and how retries/backoff should interplay with streaming; ship presets in SDKs and document guidance in the Console and quickstarts.

Scope: Cross‑SDK changes that update default config, example snippets, and docs. No breaking API surface changes—presets are additive and default changes must be opt‑in for GA. Implementation tasks include compatibility tests, language sample code, load test scenarios, and a short migration guide for customers.

Non‑goals: Changing protocol behavior or server timeouts. Not addressing lower‑level kernel tuning or OS TCP stack changes.
acceptance_criteria: Three transport presets (conservative, balanced, aggressive) documented and added as named configs in Python/TS/Go SDKs
Per‑language README examples for: connection timeout, request timeout, idle/stream keep‑alive, max connections, per‑host connection cap, and retry/backoff policy
End‑to‑end tests that validate streaming recovery semantics with transient network failures under each preset
Load test report comparing balanced vs current defaults showing no regression in throughput and improved median tail latency for typical RLHF chat workloads
Docs page in SDK docs and a short Console guidance doc linked from onboarding
tasks: Design canonical presets and rationale (latency vs cost tradeoffs)
Add named presets & config builder to Python SDK
Add named presets & config builder to TypeScript SDK
Add named presets & config builder to Go SDK
Create three language quickstart snippets illustrating streaming with retries and keep‑alive
Write unit + integration tests for connection pooling behavior
Run load tests (internal harness) and produce benchmark summary
Update SDK changelogs and migration notes
Author Console guidance doc and link to SDK examples
design_notes: Presets should be additive and non‑breaking. Default runtime behavior remains unchanged until opt‑in via an environment variable (SDK_TRANSPORT_PRESET) for beta users.

Presets include five logical knobs: connect_timeout, request_timeout, stream_idle_timeout (keep‑alive), max_connections, max_connections_per_host. Retries/backoff are suggested but orthogonal—examples will recommend backoff ceilings tied to request_timeout.
Streaming semantics: advise on 'no automatic full‑response retries' for long‑running streams. Instead recommend resumable streaming where possible and idempotency tokens for request-level retries.

Language differences: Go's net/http keeps connections differently; examples will use Transport.MaxIdleConns and IdleConnTimeout. Python will show both requests/urllib3 and asyncio aiohttp patterns. TS will include fetch + agent (Node http.Agent) and browser guidance.

Observability: include knobs to emit metrics for connection pool usage, per‑request timeout triggers, and retry counts to Console telemetry so customers can tune presets against observed workload patterns.
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Changing defaults could regress existing customers. Mitigation: defaults remain unchanged for now; presets are opt‑in and we experiment with opt‑in beta customers only.
Risk: Language runtime differences make parity hard. Mitigation: create minimal common contract and per‑SDK adapters; run cross‑language compatibility e2e tests.
Risk: Users misconstrue streaming retries. Mitigation: explicit docs and examples demonstrating common failure modes and recommended patterns (resumable streams, idempotency tokens).
implementation_details: Python: add TransportPreset class in redwood_sdk.transport with factory methods .conservative()/.balanced()/.aggressive() that return a simple dataclass mapping to underlying HTTPX/urllib3/aiohttp settings.
TypeScript: add TransportPresets export in @redwood/sdk that configures node http.Agent and fetch timeouts; include browser fallback notes for keep‑alive behavior.
Go: provide TransportPreset type that maps to http.Transport fields (MaxIdleConns, IdleConnTimeout, TLSHandshakeTimeout, ResponseHeaderTimeout) and helper to attach to client with retry middleware.
All SDKs should expose a single telemetry event when a preset is applied for internal rollout visibility (opt‑out by env var).
Testing: create simulated network harness that injects TCP resets, slow responses, and mid‑stream truncations to validate streaming recovery guidance.
examples_snippets: Python balanced preset example: from redwood_sdk import Client, TransportPreset; client = Client(transport=TransportPreset.balanced())  # shows connect=200ms, request=60s, idle_keepalive=90s, max_conn=50

TypeScript aggressive preset example: import {createClient, TransportPresets} from '@redwood/sdk'; const client = createClient({ transport: TransportPresets.aggressive() }); // connect=100ms, request=30s, keepAlive=30s, maxSockets=200

Go conservative preset example: preset := transport.PresetConservative(); client := http.Client{Transport: preset.ToHTTPTransport() } // MaxIdleConns=20, IdleConnTimeout=120s, ResponseHeaderTimeout=90s
notes: Related tickets to reference during review: ENG-7423 (crosssdk transport tuning request timeouts) and ENG-11321 (unified transport config guidelines). This ticket consolidates presets + language examples and is intentionally broader UX/QA work.
We should coordinate with docs engineering for a new SDK transport page and notify Solutions and Customer Success about the beta so they can steer customers with high throughput needs.
Performance runbook: when customers report high 5xxs after changing presets, check socket exhaustion, threadpool saturation (python), and agent socket reuse (node).
